result: Mice successfully learned the association between a visual cue and reward delivery in an appetitive classical conditioning task, as evidenced by significantly reduced reaction times (Day 1: 742.8 ± 25.4 ms; Day N+1: 544.7 ± 13.0 ms; p=8.52×10⁻⁸) and miss rates (Day 1: 0.39 ± 0.04; Day N+1: 0.03 ± 0.01; p=6.37×10⁻⁹) after an average of 5.7 ± 0.4 training days. Mice also developed robust anticipatory licking responses on omission trials after learning that were absent in naïve animals.
evaluation: Claims C21-C24 provide converging behavioral evidence of successful learning with appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, n=27 mice), clear pre-post comparisons, and multiple behavioral metrics (reaction time, miss rate, anticipatory licking). The data demonstrate both improved performance and learned anticipatory responses consistent with classical conditioning.

result: In lobule simplex, mesoscale calcium imaging revealed that Cspk activity shifted from following reward delivery in naïve animals (p=5×10⁻¹⁹) to preceding reward delivery after learning (p=3.3×10⁻¹⁰⁰), with significantly decreased latency (p=1.04×10⁻⁶). After learning, Cspk responses occurred with identical timing on both rewarded and omission trials (383 ± 15 ms vs 378 ± 19 ms, p=0.78), and the shift in Cspk timing (441 ms) exceeded the change in lick timing (185 ms).
evaluation: Claims C25-C32 demonstrate a clear temporal shift in Cspk responses with learning using mesoscale imaging data with appropriate statistical tests and adequate sample sizes (5-6 mice, 74-749 trials). The comparison of Cspk timing shift to lick timing shift (C31) provides important control evidence that responses are not simply motor-related. The identical timing on rewarded vs omission trials (C32) supports a reward prediction interpretation.

result: When reward was delivered unexpectedly after learning in lobule simplex, Cspk activity followed reward delivery with significantly delayed timing compared to expected reward trials (366.1 ± 31 ms vs 793 ± 31 ms, p=2.40×10⁻⁴), and this latency was equivalent to responses in naïve animals (p=0.38).
evaluation: Claims C33-C34 provide evidence that unexpected rewards elicit responses similar to naïve animals, supporting the interpretation that learned responses represent reward prediction rather than reward per se. The statistical comparisons are appropriate (paired and two-sample t-tests, n=5 mice) and the logic is sound.

result: Two-photon imaging in lobule simplex confirmed mesoscale findings, showing significantly elevated Cspk rates following reward in naïve animals (n=1040 dendrites, p=5.5×10⁻⁴⁸) but not on omission trials (p=0.98). After learning, significantly elevated Cspk rates occurred prior to reward on both rewarded (n=906 dendrites, p=2.3×10⁻⁶⁰) and omission trials (p=1.4×10⁻³³), while post-reward rates were significantly reduced (p=2.0×10⁻¹⁹). No Cspk responses were reliably suppressed below baseline after expected reward on omission trials.
evaluation: Claims C35-C39 provide cellular-resolution confirmation of mesoscale findings with large sample sizes (906-1040 dendrites, 15-16 mice) and highly significant statistical tests. The absence of suppressed responses on omission trials (C39) is an important negative finding that argues against temporal difference error signaling, though this interpretation requires caution as absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

result: In lobule simplex after learning, a minority of PC dendrites (204/906, 23%) exhibited significant post-reward responses and also responded to the visual cue (p=5.9×10⁻³⁶), while the majority (702/906, 77%) only responded to the reward-predicting cue without post-reward responses (p=3.9×10⁻³⁶).
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 provide important population-level analysis showing heterogeneity in PC dendrite responses. The statistical tests are appropriate and the large sample size (906 dendrites) provides confidence. This suggests incomplete transition of responses from reward to cue in a subset of neurons, which is biologically plausible during learning.

result: In lobule simplex on Day N+2, unexpected reward delivery produced significant Cspk responses (n=243 dendrites, p=1.6×10⁻⁸), while expected reward no longer produced significant post-reward responses (p=0.8). PC dendrites responsive to the reward-predicting cue (84/243) were also responsive to unexpected reward (p=2.3×10⁻¹²), suggesting the same neurons signal predictions under different conditions.
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 demonstrate that the same PC dendrites can respond to both predicted and unpredicted reward-related events, supporting flexible encoding of reward expectation. The statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (243 dendrites, 6 mice). The finding that cue-responsive dendrites also respond to unexpected reward (C45) is particularly important for understanding functional properties.

result: In lobule simplex, licking did not drive Cspk responses: there was no significant response to licking during the inter-trial interval (p=0.6, n=768 dendrites), and pre-reward Cspk timing was nearly identical on trials with early vs late licks (300 ms vs 330 ms) and on trials with high vs low lick rates (both 300 ms).
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 provide multiple lines of evidence that learned Cspk responses are not motor-related. The lick-triggered average (C46), lick timing analysis (C47), and lick rate analysis (C48) all converge on the conclusion that Cspk responses are independent of licking behavior. Sample sizes are adequate (768-906 dendrites) and the consistency across analyses strengthens the conclusion.

result: In Crus I, Cspk activity in naïve animals was sensory-related, following the visual cue on both rewarded (p=3.6×10⁻²⁰, n=133 dendrites) and omission trials (p=3.4×10⁻¹⁷). After learning, cue responses were significantly enhanced (p=2.3×10⁻⁸, n=178 dendrites), while reward responses remained weak or non-significant both before and after learning.
evaluation: Claims C49-C51 demonstrate that Crus I exhibits a different pattern than lobule simplex, with sensory-driven responses that are enhanced by reward association. Statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (133-178 dendrites, 6-7 mice). This functional compartmentalization across cerebellar regions is an important finding.

result: In Crus I, unexpected reward produced no Cspk response in naïve animals but elicited a large response after learning (p=5.1×10⁻¹¹, n=141 dendrites). PC dendrites that were cue-responsive (100/141) also showed robust responses to unexpected reward (p=7.7×10⁻¹¹).
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 show that Crus I develops unexpected reward responses only after establishing reward expectation, contrasting with lobule simplex. The statistical tests are appropriate and the finding that cue-responsive dendrites also respond to unexpected reward supports flexible expectation signaling. Sample sizes are adequate (141 dendrites, 5 mice).

result: In Crus I, Cspk responses were independent of licking: no significant response to ITI licks in naïve animals (p=0.04, n=93 dendrites), and after learning, cue-evoked Cspk timing (230 ms) and amplitude were largely independent of both lick timing (p=0.04) and lick rate (p=0.4).
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 demonstrate that Crus I responses, like lobule simplex, are not motor-related. Multiple control analyses converge on this conclusion with appropriate statistical tests. The p-value for C54 (p=0.04) is marginal and the authors appropriately interpret this as non-significant given the one-tailed test and context.

result: In Crus II, Cspk rates were elevated following reward in naïve animals (p=2.7×10⁻¹⁸, n=147 dendrites) but not on omission trials (p=1.0). After learning, robust cue responses emerged on both rewarded (p=9.7×10⁻²⁶, n=245 dendrites) and omission trials (p=6.1×10⁻²¹), but unlike lobule simplex, reward responses persisted after learning (p=5.6×10⁻¹¹) with no significant increase on omission trials at expected reward time (p=0.95).
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 demonstrate that Crus II exhibits yet another distinct pattern, with both cue and reward responses persisting after learning. Statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (147-245 dendrites, 5-6 mice). This further supports functional compartmentalization across lateral cerebellar regions.

result: In Crus II, unexpected reward after learning produced enhanced Cspk rates compared to expected reward (p=1.1×10⁻¹¹, n=184 dendrites). PC dendrites responsive to the cue (60/184) continued to respond to both expected (p=1.5×10⁻⁴) and unexpected reward (p=1.1×10⁻¹⁵).
evaluation: Claims C61-C62 show that Crus II responses scale with expectation while maintaining reward responsiveness. Statistical tests are appropriate and the finding that the same dendrites respond to cue, expected reward, and unexpected reward (C62) demonstrates complex encoding properties. Sample sizes are adequate (184 dendrites, 6 mice).

result: In Crus II, naïve animals showed significant lick-related Cspk responses during ITI (p=1.6×10⁻⁵, n=104 dendrites), but these disappeared after learning (p=0.98, n=136 dendrites). After learning, pre-reward Cspk timing was independent of both lick timing (300 ms for early and late licks) and lick rate (300 ms for high and low rates).
evaluation: Claims C63-C66 show that while Crus II has motor-related responses in naïve animals (consistent with prior literature), learned responses are not motor-driven. The disappearance of lick responses after learning (C64) is particularly interesting and suggests task-dependent modulation. Statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample sizes.

result: Using a piezoelectric sensor to measure body movement, there was no relationship between learned Cspk responses and movement in any of the three regions (LS: p=0.13, n=316 dendrites; Crus I: p=0.13, n=27 dendrites; Crus II: p=0.10, n=97 dendrites), supporting the conclusion that learned responses are driven by the reward-predictive visual cue rather than movement-related reafference.
evaluation: Claims C67 and C80 provide important control data using an independent movement measurement method. The piezoelectric sensor is described as extremely sensitive (detecting breathing), making this a strong control. Sample sizes vary across regions (27-316 dendrites) with Crus I having the smallest sample, but all show consistent null results. This strengthens the interpretation that responses are sensory/cognitive rather than motor.

result: Imaging Cspk activity across learning sessions suggests that the same climbing fibers that respond to reward in naïve animals can shift to respond to the reward-predictive cue after learning, based on tracking experiments attempting to identify the same PC dendrites across days.
evaluation: Claim C88 is based on tracking experiments (Figure 4) that attempt to identify the same neurons across learning. However, the authors acknowledge significant limitations: 'we cannot rule out a contribution of sensory gating due to arousal' and note that their tracking approach 'cannot provide definitive evidence' due to close spacing of PC dendrites. While they use both manual and automated approaches with stringent overlap criteria (>50%), the inherent uncertainty in cell tracking across days, combined with the possibility of arousal-related gating, makes this conclusion uncertain rather than definitively supported.

result: No Cspk responses were reliably suppressed below baseline after expected reward on omission trials in any of the three regions, suggesting that Cspk responses may not instruct a strict temporal difference (TD) learning model in this paradigm.
evaluation: Claims C39, C89, and C90 report the absence of negative prediction error signals (suppressed responses on omission trials). While the authors appropriately describe their methods for detecting suppression and report null findings, absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The authors themselves note this is speculative (C90 is marked as SPECULATION/INFERENCE) and discuss alternative explanations including that negative prediction errors might emerge with overtraining (citing Coddington and Dudman, 2018) or exist in other cerebellar regions. The conclusion about TD learning is therefore uncertain rather than definitively supported or refuted.

result: All three lateral cerebellar regions (lobule simplex, Crus I, and Crus II) exhibited learned Cspk responses related to reward prediction, but with distinct patterns: LS showed responses that shifted from reward to cue with learning; Crus I showed enhanced sensory responses when the cue was associated with reward; and Crus II showed both cue and reward responses persisting after learning. These differences suggest that learned changes are overlaid on pre-existing sensory and motor signals unique to each region, enabling the lateral cerebellum to harness distinct signals for different forms of learning.
evaluation: Claims C4 and C81-C87 synthesize the major findings across all three regions. The experimental evidence from claims C25-C66 strongly supports the distinct patterns in each region. The interpretation that learned changes are overlaid on pre-existing signals (C86) is a reasonable inference from the data, though marked as IMPLICIT/INFERENCE. The broader speculation about enabling different learning strategies (C87) is more speculative but is appropriately framed as interpretation rather than direct observation.

result: Classical models of cerebellar learning posit that climbing fibers operate according to a supervised learning rule, with signals from the inferior olive instructing changes in motor output by signaling movement errors.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C12 accurately describe established classical models with appropriate citations to foundational work (Albus, 1971; Ito, 1972; Marr, 1969). These are well-established facts in the field and serve as important context for the current findings.

result: The cerebellum contributes to non-motor processes including cognition, social processing, aggression, and emotion, and cerebellar deficits are associated with autism spectrum disorders, language processing deficits, and schizophrenia. The cerebellum also modulates reward association pathways in the VTA.
evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C5-C11 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These establish important context for why studying reward-related cerebellar signals is relevant. The claims are well-supported by the cited literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

result: Accumulating evidence demonstrates that climbing fibers exhibit diverse responses beyond motor error signals, including temporal-difference error signals and reward prediction signals, and cerebellar granule cells can display reward-related signals.
evaluation: Claims C13-C15 and C19-C20 accurately summarize recent literature with appropriate citations. These establish that the field has moved beyond classical error-based models and provide important context for the current study. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of prior work is accurate.

result: Anatomical and functional studies have identified pathways from the lateral cerebellum to reward-related structures: a disynaptic pathway to the striatum and a direct monosynaptic connection from the lateral cerebellum via deep cerebellar nuclei to VTA dopamine neurons. Activating these DCN-VTA projections is sufficient to modulate reward-driven behaviors and these projections are endogenously active under social conditions.
evaluation: Claims C16-C18 and C77-C79 accurately describe anatomical and functional connectivity with appropriate citations (Hoshi et al., 2005; Carta et al., 2019). These provide crucial context for why cerebellar reward signals would be functionally relevant. The characterization of prior work is accurate and the citations are appropriate.

result: Prior work has shown that the lateral cerebellar regions studied (LS, Crus I, Crus II) receive diverse sensory and motor inputs and have been implicated in both motor and non-motor behaviors, with connectivity to multiple downstream targets including cortical areas, hippocampus, and striatum.
evaluation: Claims C68-C75 accurately summarize prior literature on the functional properties and connectivity of the lateral cerebellar regions with appropriate citations. This provides important context for interpreting the functional compartmentalization observed in the current study. The characterization of prior work is accurate.

result: Methodological validation from prior work supports that: (1) Cspk responses to licking are localized primarily to Crus II; (2) mesoscale calcium imaging of PC dendrites expressing GCaMP6f accurately reports Cspk activity; and (3) calcium transient amplitude variability reflects climbing fiber input properties rather than combined climbing fiber and parallel fiber signals.
evaluation: Claims C76, C92, and C93 cite appropriate prior work to validate methodological approaches. These are important for establishing that the imaging methods used can accurately report the signals of interest. The citations are appropriate (Heffley et al., 2018; Gaffield et al., 2016, 2018, 2019; Welsh et al., 1995).

result: Prior work in the mesolimbic dopamine system has shown that: (1) dopamine release is governed by correct movement initiation rather than simply reward prediction in operant tasks; (2) increased firing to reward can persist after learning; (3) negative prediction errors emerge very late in training; and (4) VTA dopamine neurons have different response profiles depending on their striatal projection target.
evaluation: Claims C94-C97 accurately cite relevant prior work on VTA dopamine signaling with appropriate citations (Syed et al., 2016; Coddington and Dudman, 2018; Menegas et al., 2017; Parker et al., 2016). These comparisons to the dopamine system provide useful context for interpreting the cerebellar findings and discussing alternative explanations for the absence of negative prediction errors.

result: The learned reward-predictive Cspk signals observed are consistent with a model in which cerebellar output could provide information about rewarding stimuli to downstream structures like VTA and striatum. If combined with mossy fiber contextual information, such signals could instruct plasticity to depress Purkinje cell output and enable DCN output to VTA in response to reward-associated stimuli or actions.
evaluation: Claims C91 and C98-C101 present interpretive models and speculation about functional implications. While these are reasonable interpretations given the data and known circuitry, they are explicitly speculative (marked as SPECULATION/INFERENCE). The proposed model (C101) about how Cspk signals could instruct plasticity is plausible but not directly tested. These represent important discussion points and hypotheses for future work rather than supported conclusions from the current data.
